slides: Open by defining affine geometry as the geometry that keeps incidence, parallelism, ratios along parallel directions, barycentric combinations, and determinant-controlled area, while giving up Euclidean angle and length. The chapter is about learning which facts survive that trade.

Use the route slide to organize a broad chapter. The lecture begins with parallelism and Desargues, then tracks dilatations and half-turns, compares affinities with equiaffinities, tests a shear lab, reads lattice area through Pick and Farey data, and ends with barycentric and three-dimensional affine coordinates.

Parallelism is the central invariant on this slide. The translated triangle keeps corresponding sides parallel and connector vectors equal, while the centrally perspective pair sends connector lines through one point. Desargues turns those parallel and perspective observations into an affine incidence theorem.

The proof dependency scaffold reminds students that affine geometry is not a list of disconnected tricks. The chapter builds from order and parallelism through Desargues, dilatations, affinities, equiaffinities, lattices, barycentric coordinates, and finally three-dimensional lattice structure.

Dilatations are the bridge between familiar Euclidean transformations and affine transformations. A central dilatation scales area by the square of its scale, translations preserve displacement vectors, and composing two half-turns produces a translation with the expected vector.

Affinities preserve lines and parallelism, but their determinant controls area. The general affinity scales area by one point one one five, while the equiaffine shear and hyperbolic stretch keep determinant one. This separates affine incidence from equiaffine area preservation.

The shear lab makes equiaffinity operational. Thirteen shear parameters are sampled, every determinant remains one, and the signed area stays at zero point seven five seven five to roundoff. This is a useful antidote to thinking shear must distort all measurements.

The lattice slide uses affine area in a discrete setting. The polygon has shoelace area nineteen point five, boundary count nine, and interior count sixteen, so Pick's theorem lands exactly. The Farey sequence adds visible primitive directions with adjacent determinant one.

Barycentric coordinates express affine position without choosing an origin. The sample point has weights zero point two two, zero point three three, and zero point four five, summing to one, and reconstructs with zero error. Ceva and Menelaus encode incidence through products.

Close by lifting affine ideas into three dimensions. A lattice basis has unit-cell volume one point one six five five, unimodular changes preserve volume, and rational planes are detected by integer coefficients. The chapter's moral is that affine geometry is geometry by preserved linear structure.
